35.7706,-78.63276: John Chavis Ca. 1762 1838. African American teacher, preacher, & Revolutionary War veteran. Taught free black & prominent white students in school nearby.
35.77166,-78.65331: Dorothea Dix Hospital. Authorized 1849, largely through work of Dorothea L. Dix, crusader for better care of the mentally ill. 500 yards southwest.
35.7721,-78.63777: Shaw University. Founded 1865 by Baptist missionary Henry Martin Tupper. Chartered 1875; named for benefactor Elijah Shaw of Mass.
35.7728,-78.63528: James H. Young 1860 1921. Colonel of black N.C. regiment in war with Spain; edited Raleigh Gazette; legislator. Home was 25 ft. W.
35.7733,-78.64631: Edward A. Johnson 1860 1944. Politician, businessman, philanthropist, author, and educator. First black to publish a N.C. textbook. Home was here.
35.77442,-78.64201: Thomas R. Jernigan 1847 1920. U.S. negotiator in China for 30 years. Consul in Japan and China. Editor, author, and lawyer. His home was 2 blocks E.
35.77503,-78.63513: James H. Harris 1832 1891. Black legislator & orator; member 1868 convention; a founder of Republican Party & Union League in N.C. Home was 1 block W.
35.77568,-78.64198: Gales Family. Joseph, Raleigh Register founder, 1799; his wife Winifred, early novelist; sons Joseph and Weston, editors, lived 2 blks. E.
35.77798,-78.64192: William W. Holden 1818 1892. Editor. Appointed provisional governor, 1865. Elected governor, 1868; impeached and removed, 1871. Home stood here.
35.7786,-78.66376: The Governor Morehead School. Established for visually impaired students in 1845 under leadership of John Motley Morehead. Present plant is 500 yards north.
35.77938,-78.64016: First Presbyterian Church. Organized 1816. Site of Constitutional Convention of 1835. State Supreme Court met here, 1831-40, after Capitol fire. This building completed 1900.
35.7796,-78.63845: Andrew Johnson 1808 1875. President of the United States, 1865-69. Born near here in a kitchen now located 1 mile N.E.
35.77965,-78.63938: State Capitol. Built 1833-40. Ithiel Towne, A. J. Davis and David Paton, architects. First State House built here, 1796; burned, 1831.
35.78006,-78.63649: State Bank Building. First State Bank, est. 1814; housed Christ Church rectory, 1873-1951. Reopened 1969 as bank 50 yds. N.W.
35.78053,-78.64334: L. O'b. Branch. Confederate brigadier general; president of Raleigh and Gaston Railroad, 1852-55; member of Congress, 1855-61. Home here, grave 2/3 mi. east.
35.78059,-78.62222: St. Agnes. Hospital. First nursing school in N.C. for African Americans, 1896-1961. Founded by Sarah Hunter. Building four blocks N.
35.7806,-78.64554: Freedmen's Convention. Delegates resolved to seek equal rights for state's freed blacks. Met, Sept. 29-Oct. 3, 1865, one block north.
35.78069,-78.62222: St. Augustine's College. Founded in 1867 by the Episcopal Church as a normal school for freedmen. Since 1928 a four-year college. 4 blocks N.
35.78081,-78.63227: Anna J. Cooper 1858 1964. Educator, orator, & early black feminist. Graduate, St. Augustine's. Author, A Voice from the South (1892). Grave 2 1/2 blks. S.
35.78082,-78.64955: William Boylan. President of Raleigh and Gaston Railroad; president of the State Bank; publisher of the Raleigh "Minerva" 1803-1810. Home is 3 blks. S.W.
35.7809,-78.65061: Joel Lane House. Built prior to 1770 and often site of political meetings. Decision to locate Raleigh on Lane's land made there, 1792. Stands 2 blocks south.
35.78119,-78.63777: John S. Ravenscroft. First Episcopal Bishop of the Diocese of N.C., 1823-1830. Active in the revival of the Church. Interred in church 50 yds. south.
35.78119,-78.63871: Medical Society Of North Carolina. Successor to earlier group founded in 1799. Formed here in 1849. Dr. Edmund Strudwick was first president.
35.78121,-78.63946: North Carolina Dental Society. Organized in 1856 in the Guion Hotel, which stood here. Dr. W. F. Bason, Haw River, first president.
35.78122,-78.63962: North Carolina Bar Association. Organized here, Feb. 10, 1899, in room then used by N.C. Supreme Court. Platt Walker of Charlotte, group's first president.
35.78154,-78.65316: Saint Mary's. Episcopal school for girls. Established 1842 by Rev. Aldert Smede on the site of an earlier Episcopal boys school.
35.78235,-78.638: North Carolina Museum Of History. Collection gathered by Fred Olds merged 1902 with state's artifacts to create Hall of History. Moved here in 1994.
35.78248,-78.64: N.C. State Museum Of Natural Sciences. Collection began with 1851 geological survey; a museum since 1879; H. H. Brimley, curator from 1895 to 1946.
35.78249,-78.63698: N.C. Office Of Archives And History. Organized as the N.C. Historical Commission in 1903; R. D. W. Connor, first secretary. Moved to this building, 1968.
35.7825,-78.6372: North Carolina State Library. Established 1812 under Wm. Hill, Sec. of State; James F. Taylor first state librarian, 1843. Moved here in 1968.
35.78282,-78.59253: Clarence Poe 1881 1964. Editor and publisher of the Progressive Farmer, 1903-1954. Social and agricultural reformer. Lived 400 yards S.E.
35.78327,-78.65596: The Governor Morehead School. Established for visually impaired students in 1845 under leadership of John Motley Morehead. Present plant is 3 blocks south.
35.78391,-78.64162: Artificial Limbs. North Carolina was first state to provide limbs to Confederate amputees. Factory, which operated 1866-67, was 1/4 mi. NE.
35.78439,-78.63622: Fannie E. S. Heck 1862 1915. Social activist; writer. Led the Baptist Woman's Missionary Union after 1892. A benefactor of present Meredith College. Lived in this house
35.7846,-78.65852: Camp Bryan Grimes. Spanish-American War camp, 95 acres, named for the Confederate general, was located here. Only U.S. Army camp in the state, 1898.
35.78461,-78.63788: Raleigh And Gaston Railroad. Chartered in 1835 and completed in 1840. Length 85 miles. Its southern terminus was 400 ft. W.
35.78464,-78.63457: Oakwood Cemetery. Governors Aycock, Bragg, Fowle, Holden, Swain, and Worth, other notables and Confederates buried there. 3 blocks E.
35.78468,-78.63792: W. N. H. Smith. N.C. Chief Justice, 1878-1889; state legislator; U.S. & Confederate Congressman. Home was one blk. W.; grave 3/4 mi. E.
35.78469,-78.63457: John L. Taylor 1769 1829. First Chief Justice of N.C. Supreme Court, 1819-1829; author of numerous legal works. Grave is 1/2 mi. E. Home is 1 mi. S.W.
35.78471,-78.6362: William Polk 1758 1834. Revolutionary War officer; first president of State Bank, 1811-19. In 1825 hosted Lafayette in house that stood here.
35.78608,-78.63608: Jane Mc Kimmon 1867 1957. Home economist. From 1911 to 1937 she organized and led N.C.'s home demonstration program. Lived here.
35.78644,-78.66338: North Carolina State University At Raleigh. Chartered 1887. Opened 1889 as a land grant college. Since 1931 campus of Consolidated University.
35.78801,-78.63841: Peace College. Founded by Presbyterian elder Wm. Peace 1857 as school for women; opened 1872. Main building used as Confederate hospital & by Freedmen's Bureau.
35.78804,-78.66944: N.C. Colored State Fair. Operated 1879-1930 by N.C. Industrial Assoc. to accommodate the state's black citizens. Was held, 1891-1925, fifty yds. N.
35.79285,-78.64684: Methodist Orphanage. Est. by Methodist Church, 1899; served children in central & eastern N.C. Campus here until 1979.
35.79403,-78.63152: Old Breastworks. Breastworks were thrown up around Raleigh, 1863, by order of Governor Vance, for protection against Federal raids. Remains are 1/3 mile W.
35.79439,-78.70663: North Carolina State Fair. Agricultural fair. Was first held in 1853 and moved to this location, its third, in 1928.
35.79441,-78.68876: Meredith College. An independent women's college chartered 1891 as Baptist Female University. Named 1909 for education advocate Thos. Meredith. Campus here since 1926.
35.79818,-78.70817: Fairgrounds Speedway. After 1928 popularized Indy-style car racing. Site hosted the last NASCAR race on dirt track, 1970. Half-mile oval was 250 yds. SW.
35.81234,-78.65105: Willis Smith. United States Senator, 1950-53, speaker N.C. House of Representatives, president American Bar Assn. Home is 100 yds. W., grave is two miles S.E.
35.90063,-78.88804: Rural Credit Union. Lowes Grove credit union, first in South, formed to serve local farmers. Est. Dec. 9, 1915, on initiative of John Sprunt Hill.
35.9563,-78.89179: Rose Butler Browne 1897 1986. Educator & civil rights activist. Chair, Education Dept., N.C. College for Negroes, 1948-63. Her grave is 100 yds. N.E.
35.95915,-78.91057: John Merrick 1859 1919. Black business leader. In 1898 he founded what is now N.C. Mutual Life Insurance Company. His grave is 85 yds. N.W.
35.97014,-78.93257: James E. Shepard. Negro educational and religious leader. Founder of a college (1910), now N.C. Central University, its president to 1947. Grave is 1 1/2 miles S.E.
35.97524,-78.89337: North Carolina Central University. Founded 1910 by James E. Shepard for Negroes. State liberal arts college, 1925-1969. Now a regional university.
35.98236,-78.89893: Bull City Blues. During the 1920s-1940s, Durham was home to African American musicians whose work defined a distinctive regional style. Blues artists often played in the surrounding Hayti community and downtown tobacco warehouse district. Prominent among these were Blind Boy Fuller (Fulton Allen) (1907-1941) and Blind Gary Davis (1896-1972), whose recordings influenced generations of players.
35.98963,-78.90904: John Sprunt Hill 1869 1961. Banker and attorney. Leader in credit union movement. Benefactor, UNC Library. Lived here.
35.99565,-78.90015: Black Wall Street. In the early decades of the 1900s, Durham acquired national reputation for entrepreneurship. Businesses owned by African Americans lined Parrish Street. Among them were N.C. Mutual Life Insurance Co. (moved to Parrish, 1906), led by John Merrick, Dr. Aaron Moore, & C. C. Spaulding, and Mechanics and Farmers Bank (1907), led by R. B. Fitzgerald and W. G. Pearson.
35.99685,-78.91569: Pauli Murray 1910 1985. First African American female Episcopal priest; lawyer, activist, poet, & human rights champion. Wrote Proud Shoes, 1956. Childhood home ¼ mi. S.
